title: Why is the word "dog" such a mystery? | ANIMAL WORDS

entries.note: A living, breathing thing; its Latin root may specify non-human creatures, though in 14th-century English it could include humans, with [[see:beast]]s set apart.
Recalled from the previous episode as basically any living thing, in contrast with [[see:animal]], which also breathes.
In 14th-century English, beasts were the living, breathing things other than humans, unlike [[see:animal]], which could include people.
Refers to animals with mammary glands that suckle their young; related to [[same-root:mama]] and to the place name [[same-root:Manchester]].
Related to [[same-root:mammal]] through the idea of the mammary gland.
A place name covered in a recent Rob video, linked to the mammary gland and [[same-root:mammal]] because of nearby breast-shaped hills.
Literally means flat-footed and has the same ending as [[see:octopus]], so it can be pluralised platypuses, platypi or platypodes.
Built from Greek elements for eight and foot but not a Greek word; octopuses, octopi and octopodes all have precedent, though Rob prefers octopuses.
Rob's example of choosing an English plural over the Latin stadia, as he does with [[see:octopus]].
Rob's example of choosing an English plural over the Latin referenda, as he does with [[see:octopus]].
The actual Greek name for the octopus, meaning many-footed; it passed through Latin into English, was used for cuttlefish and gave [[gave:polyp]].
A medical term inspired by [[from:polypus]] because it looks like a sea creature attached to the body; its plural is murky, sometimes recorded as polypi.
An example of the Latin -i plural that justifies octopi as a plural of [[see:octopus]].
An example of the Latin -i plural that justifies octopi as a plural of [[see:octopus]].
Has the same foot element as [[see:octopus]] but takes an English plural, isopods, showing that English doesn't use Greek plurals.
An example of an English plural for a word ending in -us, which supports octopuses as a plural of [[see:octopus]].
An example of an English plural for a word ending in -us, which supports octopuses as a plural of [[see:octopus]].
From Latin [[from:repere]], to crawl, describing animals that keep low to the ground.
Literally double life, from Greek amphi and bios as in biology; related to the Latin prefix [[same-root:ambi-]].
A Latin prefix meaning both, related to the amphi- in [[same-root:amphibian]].
Theatres with seating on both sides; the amphi- prefix can mean all but also specifically both, as in [[same-root:amphibian]].
Able to use both hands; literally right-handed on both sides, from [[from:ambi-]].
Latin for left-handed, mentioned while unpicking the right-handedness in [[see:ambidextrous]].
Covers a vast array of animals; Old English fisc, sharing an ancient root with Latin piscis and [[same-root:Pisces]], and found across Indo-European languages.
The star sign, which shares an ancient root with [[same-root:fish]].
First recorded in the 1400s meaning scoundrel or swindler and only used for the fish from the 1700s; origin uncertain, probably Germanic.
One of the specific names older English used before it had a general word like [[see:shark]].
One of the specific names older English used before it had a general word like [[see:shark]].
An older specific name that is still used for a type of [[see:shark]].
A less scary English name for the hammerhead [[see:shark]], in use until at least the 1740s.
The Old Norse word for [[equivalent:shark]], related to the Dutch [[same-root:haai]] and the German [[same-root:Hai]].
The Dutch word for [[equivalent:shark]], related to the Old Norse [[same-root:hár]].
The German word for [[equivalent:shark]], related to the Old Norse [[same-root:hár]].
The French word for [[equivalent:shark]], which Jess says has a scary meaning (garbled in the captions).
The Greek word for [[equivalent:shark]], literally jagged biter.
An old seafaring term for a [[see:shark]] that Rob once came across.
What [[see:Herman Melville]] called brown sharks in one of his books (not Moby-Dick), similar to [[see:water lawyer]].
[[see:Herman Melville]]'s name for the white [[see:shark]].
Lacking vertebrae, the joints of the spine; [[from:vertebra]] means joint, so invertebrates are literally spineless.
From a Latin verb meaning to cut into, hence segmented; the Romans translated the Greek word behind [[same-root:entomology]].
Its Greek first part means to cut into, just as [[equivalent:insect]] does in Latin; often confused with [[unrelated:etymology]].
Easily confused with [[unrelated:entomology]], which is the basis of a joke Jess is told almost daily.
From the Greek word for spider; the group also includes scorpions, mites and ticks.
Praying as in to a god, not preying; mantis means diviner or seer, from the same root as [[same-root:mnemonic]] and [[same-root:memory]].
Shares a Proto-Indo-European root with the mantis in [[same-root:praying mantis]].
Shares a Proto-Indo-European root with the mantis in [[same-root:praying mantis]].
Shares a Proto-Indo-European root with the mantis in [[same-root:praying mantis]].
Shares a Proto-Indo-European root with the mantis in [[same-root:praying mantis]].
The scientific name of the [[see:praying mantis]], which adds to the idea of praying.
From Latin [[from:mollis]], soft; at first it meant only gooey creatures, later shelled ones too; related to [[same-root:moelleux]] and [[same-root:melt]].
A French word for oozing, soft chocolate cake or fondant, related to [[same-root:mollusk]].
Linked at a more basic level to [[same-root:mollusk]].
Thought to be a sailors' variant of [[from:squirt]], referring to the ink; a group is a shoal, though some prefer [[see:squad]].
The collective noun some people advocate for a group of [[see:squid]], instead of shoal.
From Latin [[from:calamarius]], pertaining to pens, ultimately from [[from:calamus]], reed; unrelated to [[unrelated:calligraphy]].
Means beautiful writing and is unrelated to [[unrelated:calamari]], despite Rob's first guess.
From Latin [[from:crusta]], shell, referring to hard exoskeletons, roughly the opposite of [[see:mollusk]]; includes lobsters and crabs.
Probably a euphemism meaning the brown thing, used because people were too scared to say the animal's real name, which is now lost.
The Greek word for bear; Rob half-remembers that these words may relate to honey, which would make them euphemisms like [[see:bear]].
The 'dog mystery': the word's origin is unknown; other Germanic languages use [[see:hound]]-type words, and its -og ending appears in other unexplained animal names.
A French breed name borrowed from the English [[from:dog]].
The type of word other Germanic languages use for [[see:dog]]; it shares a Proto-Indo-European root with [[same-root:canine]] and [[same-root:cynic]].
Related to [[same-root:hound]].
Means doglike, from Greek kyon; the Cynics followed [[see:Antisthenes]], perhaps for dog-like wandering lives or for teaching at [[see:Kynosarges]]; same root as [[same-root:hound]].
The philosopher the [[see:cynic]]s followed, nicknamed something like the absolute dog; he taught at [[see:Kynosarges]].
A gymnasium near Athens named the grey dog, where [[see:Antisthenes]] taught; possibly where the [[see:cynic]]s got their name.
Old English had frosc, as with German [[same-root:Frosch]] and Dutch [[same-root:vors]], but English switched to an -og form, perhaps for cuteness, as with [[see:dog]].
The German for [[equivalent:frog]], reflecting the older form that English replaced.
The Dutch for [[equivalent:frog]], reflecting the older form that English replaced.
Another unexplained -og word like [[see:dog]]; Old English hog meant the male of almost any farm animal, which argues against a Celtic origin like Welsh [[unrelated?:hwch]].
A Welsh word for a pig or sow that sounds like [[see:hog]], though the hosts doubt the connection.
Another unusual -g word like [[see:dog]]; originally meant a male deer in its fifth year, while related words elsewhere mean the male of any species.
Has no obvious Germanic source; its earliest trace is [[from?:picbred]], an acorn, perhaps meaning pig bread. Another of the [[see:dog]]-like mysteries.
The Germanic animal name paired with French-derived [[see:beef]] in the usual contrast that doesn't work so neatly for [[see:pig]].
The French-derived meat word paired with Germanic [[see:cow]] in the usual contrast that doesn't work so neatly for [[see:pig]].
The French-derived meat word paired with Germanic [[see:sheep]] in the contrast that doesn't work so neatly for [[see:pig]].
The Germanic animal name paired with [[see:mutton]] in the contrast that doesn't work so neatly for [[see:pig]].
A term for an acorn, the earliest trace of [[gave?:pig]]; possibly meaning pig bread or pig feed, since pigs like acorns.
Of unknown origin, originally brid before the letters swapped; it has no counterpart in other Germanic or Romance languages.
Means pig fish, as discussed before; one of several animal names with a [[see:pig]] hidden inside.
An Afrikaans (Dutch) word meaning earth pig.
From Old French [[from:porc espin]], spiny or thorny pig; spelled many ways over time, including Hamlet's porpentine ('quills upon the fretful porpentine').
Once much closer to [[from:alcatraz]], but probably reshaped by Latin [[from:albus]], white, because the birds are big and white.
Portuguese for pelican, presumably naming the prison rock; from Arabic [[from:al-ghattas]], sea eagle, and the source of [[gave:albatross]].
From Old French [[from:pied de grue]], foot of a crane, because forking genealogical charts looked like a crane's long toes.
From Spanish [[from:el lagarto]], the lizard; English briefly used lagarto before adding the article to the start.
Greek krokodilos, pebble worm, probably Greek folk etymology of a foreign word; cocodrill, from French and medieval Latin, was once more common in English.
Rob and Jess note that worm was once used for dragon, which makes the pebble-worm reading of [[see:crocodile]] less unflattering.
Means river horse; its -potamus part means river, as in [[same-root:Mesopotamia]].
Means between rivers, sharing its river element with [[same-root:hippopotamus]].
Another name for the seahorse, literally horse sea monster; also a seahorse-shaped part of the brain.
Shares a Proto-Indo-European root meaning water creature with [[same-root:hydra]]; sea otters were sometimes called [[see:sea ape]]s in the 17th century.
Comes from the same water-creature root as [[same-root:otter]].
A 17th-century English name for the sea [[see:otter]].
From Malay, meaning person of the forest; the hosts aren't sure whether it implies 'old man of the forest'.
From Latin [[from:lemures]], ghosts, perhaps because of their little white faces and nocturnal habits.
From Malay, literally something that rolls up.
A different animal from the bigger [[see:moose]], though moose are called elk in some parts of the world.
Bigger than the [[see:elk]] and a different animal, though called elk in some parts of the world.
The same species as the [[see:reindeer]]; caribou tend to live in North America.
The same species as the [[see:caribou]]; reindeer is the name used in Europe and elsewhere.
The humped, curly-furred American animal, sometimes called [[see:buffalo]] even though it technically isn't one.
True buffalo live outside America and look more like cows; the word can also be a place name and a verb meaning to bully.

entries.term: Buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo
entries.note: A grammatical sentence built from the animal, the city and the verb meaning to bully: bison from Buffalo whom other Buffalo bison bully also bully Buffalo bison.
A sentence that you have to go back and reread at the end, because it led you up the garden path; examples include [[see:the horse raced past the barn fell]].

entries.term: the horse raced past the barn fell
entries.note: A classic [[see:garden path sentence]] meaning the horse that was raced past the barn fell down; reaching 'fell' forces you to reinterpret it.
Has meant cat almost forever and is nearly identical across Europe; many languages also have a cute plosive-and-hiss word that's used to call cats.
Hides a cat: it means either ground lion or dwarf lion, since its first part goes back to a root meaning low down.
The French word for [[equivalent:bat]], which oddly highlights baldness rather than flight.
Refers to the animal batting its wings, unlike the French [[equivalent:chauve-souris]].
From Latin [[from:musculus]], little mouse, because flexed muscles looked like mice running under the skin; so muscular literally means mousy.
A short-lived English word meaning muscular, literally lizardy, for the same reason as [[see:muscle]]: a lizard seeming to crawl under the skin.
The German for placenta, an example of German's literal medical terms, whereas English euphemises through Greek and Latin.
From Latin [[from:peculium]], property in cattle; first meant belonging solely to, then special or distinguished (of people rich in cows), and later odd.
A hidden cow: [[see:Edward Jenner]] protected people against smallpox with cowpox, so to vaccinate is literally to cow-ify.
The doctor who developed a smallpox [[see:vaccine]] by injecting people with a small amount of cowpox.
Means pleasantly pastoral, literally cow-tending, from the Greek elements [[from:bous]] and kolos.
Lion plus [[from:panther]], since it was thought to be a hybrid; the French later added an O to leupart, so the spelling doesn't match the pronunciation.
Thought to mean something like all beasts, though that may be folk etymology of a foreign word; it forms the second half of [[gave:leopard]].
From Guarani and Tupi, where the full name means true carnivore; without the ending meaning true, it's their general word for a carnivore.
Lion's tooth, borrowed directly from French [[from:dent de lion]], referring to the jagged leaves and perhaps the mane-like yellow bloom.
The French phrase that English borrowed directly as [[gave:dandelion]].
One of the historical names for the [[see:dandelion]].
One of the historical names for the [[see:dandelion]].
A historical name for the [[see:dandelion]], like [[see:pee-a-bed]] and [[see:wet-a-bed]], perhaps because it was used as a diuretic.
A historical [[see:dandelion]] name, like [[see:piss-a-bed]], probably reflecting its use as a diuretic.
A historical [[see:dandelion]] name, like [[see:piss-a-bed]], probably reflecting its use as a diuretic.
A name for the [[see:dandelion]] in some forms of Italian, because they're yellow and grow along roadsides.
An old name for the [[see:dandelion]], meaning something like crab grass, linked to [[see:cancer]].
Discussed with [[see:karkinos]] in a previous episode.
Discussed with [[see:cancer]] in a previous episode.
One of the historical names for the [[see:dandelion]].
A historical name for the [[see:dandelion]] that Jess thinks was probably a dig at Irish people.
Badger hound, from Old High German [[from:dahs]], badger; bred to chase badgers into their holes, which explains the shape.
From the Welsh word for dwarf dog.
A Japanese breed whose name is usually translated as little brushwood dog, referring to its fur colour or the terrain it hunted in.
Said to be an ancient Sumerian word meaning plunge earth, because hunters launched the dogs off camels' backs to give them a running start.
From a Chinese word literally meaning lion dog, another lion hidden in a word, like [[see:dandelion]].
German for growler.
From Lingala, spoken in the north-eastern Congo; the full name is a phrase thought to mean dog of the villagers, a local tamed dog.
First an insult for humans meaning [[from:mutton head]], then applied to dull or sheep-worrying dogs, and now an insult to humans again.
